variants.title: Command or event?
variants.context: A command asks an owner to decide and can be rejected: CreateOrder. An event reports a committed fact in past tense: OrderCreated. Consumers must not reinterpret an event as a request that might never have happened.
variants.prompt: A message named CreateOrder arrives at the order service. What is it?
options: A command: the owner decides and may reject it.
An event reporting that an order was already created.
A query asking the service for order details.
optionFeedback: Commands ask; the owner enforces invariants and may say no.
Nothing has been committed yet, so there is no fact to report.
It asks for a state change, and a query only reads.
variants.explanation: Commands can be rejected; events cannot.

variants.title: Command or event?
variants.context: A command asks an owner to decide and can be rejected: CreateOrder. An event reports a committed fact in past tense: OrderCreated. Consumers must not reinterpret an event as a request that might never have happened.
variants.prompt: OrderCreated is published after the order commits. What may a consumer assume?
options: The fact happened; react to it, do not re-decide it.
The order might still be rolled back before it counts.
The order is proposed and still needs approval.
optionFeedback: Events report committed facts in past tense.
The publish comes after the commit, so consumers must not treat a fact as a maybe.
Approval belongs to the command stage, which finished before this event was written.
variants.hint: What tense is the name in?
variants.explanation: An event is a durable description of a fact that already happened.

variants.title: Command or event?
variants.context: A command asks an owner to decide and can be rejected: CreateOrder. An event reports a committed fact in past tense: OrderCreated. Consumers must not reinterpret an event as a request that might never have happened.
variants.prompt: A consumer receives OrderCreated and calls the order service to ask whether it should create the order. What is wrong?
options: It should ask the payment service to confirm instead.
It reinterprets a fact as a request; the order already exists.
Nothing, because a confirming read is always safe.
optionFeedback: Moving the question to another service still re-decides a fact that is already committed.
Consumers react to facts; re-deciding them creates confusion and coupling.
The extra read couples the consumer to the producer and can return a later state than the event.
variants.hint: Who owned the decision, and when was it made?
variants.explanation: Once committed and published, the fact is the contract.

variants.title: Trace the publish path
variants.context: The producer owns the decision, the broker owns transport, each consumer owns its local effect. A transactional outbox connects state and intent without a distributed transaction: decide, commit state and outbox together, publish from the outbox, apply local effects with the event ID.
variants.prompt: A CreateOrder command arrives. Put the reliable publish path in order.

items.text: Write the order and its OrderCreated outbox record in one transaction.
Validate the command, enforce the invariant, choose the order ID while the caller waits.
A relay publishes committed outbox records; a crash may resend with the same ID.
Each consumer records the event ID with its state change, then acknowledges.

variants.hint: Both the order and the intent commit together, or neither does.
variants.explanation: Decide → commit state and outbox → publish from outbox → apply local effects. One slow consumer never enters checkout latency.

variants.title: Trace the publish path
variants.context: The producer owns the decision, the broker owns transport, each consumer owns its local effect. A transactional outbox connects state and intent without a distributed transaction: decide, commit state and outbox together, publish from the outbox, apply local effects with the event ID.
variants.prompt: The relay crashes after sending but before marking the outbox record sent. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Consumers deduplicate on the event ID and apply the effect once.
The order and outbox record had committed together.
The broker now holds two deliveries of one fact.
The relay restarts and republishes the same event ID.

variants.hint: The stable ID is what survives the crash.
variants.explanation: A retry republishes the same identity, so duplicate delivery is recognizable.

variants.title: Trace the publish path
variants.context: The producer owns the decision, the broker owns transport, each consumer owns its local effect. A transactional outbox connects state and intent without a distributed transaction: decide, commit state and outbox together, publish from the outbox, apply local effects with the event ID.
variants.prompt: A team writes the order, then publishes to the broker directly from the request handler. Put the corrected path in order.

items.text: Replace the direct publish with an outbox record in the same transaction.
Add a relay that publishes committed outbox records with retries.
Make consumers idempotent on the event ID.

variants.hint: A dual write is the bug; the outbox is the fix.
variants.explanation: Direct publish after commit can lose the event if the process dies in between.

variants.title: Choose the event shape
variants.context: EDA is a style; pub-sub, retained streams, event sourcing, and CQRS solve different problems. Pub-sub when independent capabilities react; retained streams when consumers must replay; event sourcing only when the event sequence is the source of truth.
variants.prompt: Inventory, billing, and analytics each react to the same fact and never share a worker queue. Which shape?
options: Event sourcing.
Publish-subscribe.
A single work queue.
optionFeedback: Event sourcing is a persistence model, not a delivery choice.
Each subscription receives a copy.
A work queue delivers each message to one consumer.
variants.hint: Do consumers share work or each need the fact?
variants.explanation: Use pub-sub when independent capabilities react to the same fact.

variants.title: Choose the event shape
variants.context: EDA is a style; pub-sub, retained streams, event sourcing, and CQRS solve different problems. Pub-sub when independent capabilities react; retained streams when consumers must replay; event sourcing only when the event sequence is the source of truth.
variants.prompt: A new consumer must process last month’s events to build its view. Which shape?
options: CQRS alone, with a separate read model.
A retained event stream with consumer positions.
Fire-and-forget pub-sub on a live topic.
optionFeedback: CQRS separates read and write models but keeps no history to replay from.
Retained logs allow catch-up and replay within a partition's ordering scope.
A live topic drops everything published before the consumer existed.
variants.hint: Can the history be read again?
variants.explanation: Retention enables replay; define retention windows and replay authorization.

variants.title: Choose the event shape
variants.context: EDA is a style; pub-sub, retained streams, event sourcing, and CQRS solve different problems. Pub-sub when independent capabilities react; retained streams when consumers must replay; event sourcing only when the event sequence is the source of truth.
variants.prompt: Should every event-driven system make the event sequence its source of truth?
options: Yes, because storing the event log is what makes a system event-driven.
Yes, whenever the system separates reads from writes.
No. Many systems keep a state store and publish facts from it.
optionFeedback: EDA is a style of communication and puts no requirement on how state is stored.
CQRS separates the read and write models and runs fine on a plain state store.
Choose event sourcing when rebuilding state by replay is the requirement.
variants.hint: What is authoritative in your system?
variants.explanation: Event sourcing is a deliberate choice with its own costs.

variants.title: Close the right gap
variants.context: An outbox closes the database-to-broker gap; consumer idempotency closes the broker-to-effect gap. Neither replaces the other. Read “exactly once” at the full boundary: a broker transaction does not make an external effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: The database commit succeeds, then the broker publish fails. Which pattern closes this gap?
options: A broker with more replicas.
A transactional outbox.
Consumer idempotency.
optionFeedback: More replicas protect the broker but not a commit that was never published.
The outbox writes intent with the state, so publication can be retried.
Idempotency handles duplicates, not lost publishes.
variants.hint: Between which two systems did the failure occur?
variants.explanation: The outbox closes database-to-broker; idempotency closes broker-to-effect.

variants.title: Close the right gap
variants.context: An outbox closes the database-to-broker gap; consumer idempotency closes the broker-to-effect gap. Neither replaces the other. Read “exactly once” at the full boundary: a broker transaction does not make an external effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: The broker redelivers an event after a consumer timeout. Which pattern closes this gap?
options: Consumer idempotency, recording the event ID with the effect.
A transactional outbox in the consuming service.
Global ordering of the topic's partitions.
optionFeedback: Redelivery converges on one effect.
An outbox closes the producer's dual write and does nothing about redelivery downstream.
Ordering fixes the sequence of messages but still delivers the same message twice.
variants.explanation: Acknowledge only after the local transaction that records the event ID commits.

variants.title: Close the right gap
variants.context: An outbox closes the database-to-broker gap; consumer idempotency closes the broker-to-effect gap. Neither replaces the other. Read “exactly once” at the full boundary: a broker transaction does not make an external effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: A vendor promises exactly-once delivery. Does the payment API get called exactly once?
options: Yes, as long as the consumer acknowledges before the timeout.
No. Delivery guarantees stop before the external call.
Yes, the broker deduplicates every redelivery.
optionFeedback: Speed changes nothing; a crash after the API call still leaves the effect unaccounted for.
A broker transaction does not include an external API.
Broker deduplication ends at the broker, and the payment API sits outside that transaction.
variants.hint: Which boundary does the promise cover?
variants.explanation: Use an idempotency key or reconciliation at the external boundary.

variants.title: Scope the order
variants.context: Partition by the entity whose transitions must stay ordered, include an aggregate version so consumers reject stale transitions, and avoid global order unless the domain truly requires it.
variants.prompt: Order status transitions must be applied in sequence. What is the partition key?
options: customerId.
A random key.
orderId.
optionFeedback: Customer scope is broader than needed and creates hot keys.
Random keys discard order.
The entity whose transitions must stay ordered.
variants.hint: Which entity’s transitions must not interleave?
variants.explanation: Partition by the aggregate that needs local ordering.

variants.title: Scope the order
variants.context: Partition by the entity whose transitions must stay ordered, include an aggregate version so consumers reject stale transitions, and avoid global order unless the domain truly requires it.
variants.prompt: A consumer receives OrderShipped before OrderPaid for the same order due to a replay. How does it detect the stale transition?
options: By comparing producer timestamps on the two events.
An aggregate version on the event marks the stale one.
It cannot, because the broker has already reordered them.
optionFeedback: Producer clocks drift, so a later event can carry an earlier timestamp.
Versions make gaps and staleness explicit.
The consumer carries its own version check and does not depend on broker order.
variants.hint: What field tells you the expected previous state?
variants.explanation: Include an aggregate version when consumers must reject stale or skipped transitions.

variants.title: Scope the order
variants.context: Partition by the entity whose transitions must stay ordered, include an aggregate version so consumers reject stale transitions, and avoid global order unless the domain truly requires it.
variants.prompt: Should the whole platform use one globally ordered event stream?
options: Yes, a single ordered stream is simpler to reason about.
Yes, auditing needs one authoritative order.
No. Order per entity; global order limits parallelism.
optionFeedback: One stream is simpler to describe and much harder to scale or to recover.
Audit trails can be per entity with correlation IDs.
Global order is rarely necessary or affordable.
variants.explanation: Order only where the domain requires it.
